turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr Pillay. Come in, both of you, and have a seat. How are you keeping?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I am keeping reasonably well, apart from my stomach. It has been painful, and I am not sleeping as I should.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Thandi, I come in on weekdays. He's up and pacing most nights, Doctor.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, that sounds rotten. Tell me about the stomach pain in your own words. Where do you feel it?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It sits just beneath the breastbone. A burning, gnawing ache. It is not sharp, more of a grind.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when did it start?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The nights are the difficult part, if I may say so. I wake, and I simply cannot get back to sleep, and the next day is rather wasted.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will come to the sleep, I promise. The pain itself, though, when did that begin?
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was after the braai at his brother's place. That was about—
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, let me answer. Well, actually, I would put it at three weeks. It came on gradually.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): With respect, you were already complaining before that braai. Closer to a month, Doctor.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Was I? I still think it is nearer three weeks. I cannot be more precise than that, I am afraid.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): No matter. We will say somewhere between three weeks and a month. Is the pain there all the time, or does it come and go?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): It comes and goes. It is worse after supper, and if I lie flat.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does anything ease it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A little cold milk helps. And I chew those chalky tablets from the chemist.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Those are Gaviscon, the mint ones. He chews two after a meal when the pain is bad. Not after every meal.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. Any nausea with this, or vomiting?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Nothing of that sort.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the stools? Any blood, or a black colour?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood, and they are not black. They have been a little loose on some mornings, though the colour is ordinary.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your appetite?
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He hardly touches supper. I dish it up and he pushes the plate away.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): That is true, I regret to say. Food simply does not appeal at the moment.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or chills?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I feel rather washed out, but I am not hot.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I do get a sour taste in the mouth at night. I take that to be the acid coming up.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): The sour taste is useful, thank you. I also asked about chest pain, and about your breathing.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I beg your pardon. No chest pain, and my breathing is quite all right.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Can I just say, he was sick yesterday morning. I had to wash out the basin.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): You vomited?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. I must correct myself. I have been queasy on waking, and yesterday I brought up a small amount of fluid. There was no blood.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for putting that straight. How often is the queasiness?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Most mornings this past week. A cup of tea settles it. I cannot say which morning it truly began, it crept up on me.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is all right. Coming back to the sleep, how long has it been poor?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): About a month. I drop off, then the burning wakes me, and I lie awake until the birds start.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Some nights he is still up at four. After lunch he nods off in the chair. I have stopped him driving the bakkie in the afternoons.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): The bakkie, and that robot by the school, are really not a medical matter. But yes, I am tired in the afternoons.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon tiredness, noted, and we will leave the robot out of it. What regular medicines do you take?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I take the water tablet each morning, for the blood pressure. And Panado when my head is sore.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet, do you know its name, or the dose?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I am afraid I only know it as the water tablet. It is a small white one. Half a tablet, I think. The pharmacy rolls them up for me.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's hydrochlorothiazide. Half of a twenty-five milligram tablet, so twelve point five milligrams, every morning. He does not miss doses. I collect the repeats.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Excellent. And the Panado, what strength, and how often?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets of five hundred milligrams. Perhaps three times in a week, and only when a headache comes. Not every day.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines? And any allergies?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I have no allergies, as far as I know.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I did also ask whether there are any other tablets, from me or from the chemist.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that is all. I nearly started my wife's— no, I did not take hers. I thought better of it.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He had her Losec in his hand last night. I said wait for the doctor. He never swallowed it.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sensible. Do you smoke at all? And what about alcohol?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I drink only socially.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Socially can mean quite a few things. What does a usual week look like?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): A glass with supper. There was a rather nice Cabernet at the braai, from Stellenbosch, which I—
[SEG0056] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's a bottle, Doctor. A bottle of wine most nights. I put it in the trolley with the groceries. It is not a glass.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Pillay, I am not here to scold you. It just changes what I need to check. Is a bottle most nights about right?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I am sorry. A bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. Red wine, as a rule. It has been so for years.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you saying it plainly. Any history of an ulcer, liver disease, or diabetes?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. No liver trouble that anyone has mentioned to me. My father had a stomach ulcer in his later years. I do have high blood pressure, which is ongoing.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, the blood pressure we know about. Have you had any operations?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the appendix, when I was a young man. Nineteen seventy-nine, I believe, though the month escapes me entirely.
[SEG0063] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You also had the cataract, the right eye, two years ago.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, quite so. The right eye, two years ago. It settled without trouble.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I examine your abdomen? It is soft and tender just beneath the breastbone, with no guarding. I cannot feel an enlarged liver, and the bowel sounds are present.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): While you were on the machine, the blood pressure was one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two, the pulse seventy-eight, and the temperature thirty-six point six.

[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): My impression today is gastritis, with the reflux at night, and the wine is very likely aggravating it. I cannot rule out a small ulcer, but nothing on examination looks like an emergency.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Would you want me to have a scope?

[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not at this stage. I am ordering liver blood tests, given the wine most nights, and a full blood count with them. If the pain has not settled in two weeks, we might then consider a scope.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. And is there something I can take for the pain in the meantime?

[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I will start Losec, twenty milligrams, one capsule every morning, half an hour before breakfast, for four weeks. If you can bring the wine down from a bottle toward a glass, or skip some nights, that will help the stomach and the liver. And please do not take the Panado on an empty stomach.
[SEG0072] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can keep the wine for weekends, if he agrees, and I will leave the Losec next to his tea.

[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Come back in two weeks so we can go through the results. Sooner, of course, if you vomit blood, if the pain becomes severe, or if the whites of your eyes turn yellow. Reception will book those bloods for this week.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have been very kind, and I shall do my best.

interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
